title: Orthogonality Matters: Invariant Time Series Representation for Out-of-distribution Classification

problem.claim: Time series classification methods often assume that training and testing data come from the same distribution, which makes generalization to out-of-distribution time series challenging.

gap.claim: Existing approaches that aim to learn domain-agnostic features may retain domain-specific information, limiting their adaptability to out-of-distribution data.

contributions.claim: The authors introduce Invariant Time Series Representation, a model for out-of-distribution time series classification.
ITSR learns an orthogonal decomposition by projecting time series onto two sets of orthogonal axes to obtain invariant and relevant features.
ITSR theoretically ensures low similarity between invariant and relevant features, and the authors analyze the benefits of preserving their orthogonality for out-of-distribution classification.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe ITSR as a novel model.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that results on four real-world datasets show ITSR outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
The authors report that the results demonstrate the critical role of maintaining orthogonality between invariant and relevant features.

narrative_sequence.summary: Prior time series classification work commonly assumes matched training and testing distributions.
This assumption makes out-of-distribution generalization difficult, while existing approaches may retain domain-specific information in purportedly domain-agnostic features.
The paper introduces ITSR, which decomposes time series into orthogonal invariant and relevant features and optimizes them with additional tasks.
The authors examine the benefits of preserving orthogonality between invariant and relevant features for out-of-distribution classification.
The authors report results on four real-world datasets comparing ITSR with state-of-the-art methods.

unknowns: The four datasets and their characteristics are not identified.
